# LynxDB website and blog

> Query log files from the shell or keep logs on a server with a Web UI. One binary for Linux, macOS and Windows, with PPL in both modes.

The documentation is published separately at https://docs.lynxdb.org/.

---

Source: https://lynxdb.org/

[LynxDB 26.11.1 is out Release notes](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/releases/tag/v26.11.1.896-stable)

# A log database you can pipe into

Query a file or a pipe with `lynxdb query`, or run `lynxdb server` and point your shippers at it. One binary, no cluster to run, PPL in both.

[Install LynxDB](https://lynxdb.org/#install) [Read the docs](https://docs.lynxdb.org/)

## Search stored logs in the Web UI

`lynxdb server` keeps events in columnar parts on disk and serves a search page on port 3100: a histogram of the matches, a summary of every field, a live tail and each event's fields one click away. No schema to declare first.

[Run the server](https://docs.lynxdb.org/docs/getting-started/server-mode)

## How LynxDB reads and searches logs

Pipe mode and the server run one engine: the same parser, the same columnar format and the same PPL, so a query that works on a file works on the server.

### Queries as PPL pipelines

Each command works on the rows the one before it returns. About 50 OpenSearch PPL commands, and LogsQL for queries written for VictoriaLogs.

A PPL query in six steps: source=web, where status >= 500, eval slow = response\_time > 500, stats count() as errors by host and slow, sort by errors descending, head 10

### Finds fields in plain-text logs

JSON stays as sent; timestamps, key=value pairs, syslog and access-log lines are read at query time. A field may be a number in one service and a string in another.

A plain-text log line and the fields LynxDB extracts from it: \_time 2026-11-17 08:00:00.105, host web-03, level ERROR, status 502, msg GET /api/v1/users completed

### Skips log blocks a search cannot match

Sort keys, time partitions and token filters tell a search which blocks to leave unread, and counts kept with each part answer some queries without reading a row.

A search for one path against 48 storage blocks: three are read, the other 45 are skipped

## Measured on a billion events

JSONBench loads 1 billion Bluesky events as JSON and times five queries over them. Its combined score weighs the hot runs at 60%, the cold run at 20%, the size on disk and the load time at 10% each. Lower is better.

[See the raw results](https://github.com/lynxbase/ClickBench/tree/main/json/lynxdb)

AWS m6i.8xlarge. LynxDB measured on 20 November 2026 at commit ad9d7e3b; the other rows are the results published in ClickBench.

**Combined score**log scale

1.  LynxDB**×1.00**
2.  ClickHouse**×19.03**
3.  VictoriaLogs**×29.55**
4.  Elasticsearch**×65.22**
5.  OpenSearch**×399.68**

**Load time**log scale

1.  LynxDB**824 s**
2.  ClickHouse**6,042 s**
3.  VictoriaLogs**1,078 s**
4.  Elasticsearch**22,255 s**
5.  OpenSearch**64,360 s**

**Size on disk**GB

1.  LynxDB**92.7**
2.  ClickHouse**195.8**
3.  VictoriaLogs**121.4**
4.  Elasticsearch**384.7**
5.  OpenSearch**285.1**

| Hot query time | LynxDB | ClickHouse | VictoriaLogs | Elasticsearch | OpenSearch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Q1** count by collection | 0.0012 s | 0.239 s | 0.033 s | 0.618 s | 19.922 s |
| **Q2** creates and users | 0.049 s | 2.767 s | 19.155 s | 4.930 s | 59.570 s |
| **Q3** creates by hour | 0.062 s | 2.302 s | 1.521 s | 14.213 s | 412.161 s |
| **Q4** first posters | 0.0028 s | 0.757 s | 5.914 s | 3.443 s | 6.960 s |
| **Q5** longest activity | 0.063 s | 0.805 s | 8.053 s | 3.887 s | 18.367 s |

## Takes logs from the shippers you run

An existing shipper only needs LynxDB's address. Elasticsearch bulk, OTLP, Splunk HEC, Loki push and syslog arrive on their usual endpoints.

Kubernetes through Fluent Bit, Docker through its syslog driver, the OpenTelemetry Collector, Vector, Fluent Bit, Filebeat, Logstash, Splunk HEC senders, syslog daemons and files send logs to lynxdb server, which stores the 482 GB of JSON in JSONBench in 92.7 GB and answers PPL queries over them

*   Kubernetes Fluent Bit
*   Docker syslog driver
*   OpenTelemetry OTLP
*   Vector \_bulk
*   Fluent Bit \_bulk
*   Filebeat \_bulk
*   Splunk HEC HEC
*   Syslog UDP, TCP

*   NDJSON
*   CSV
*   Elasticsearch \_bulk
*   OTLP/HTTP
*   OTLP/gRPC
*   Splunk HEC
*   RFC 5424 syslog
*   RFC 3164 syslog
*   Combined access logs
*   key=value pairs
*   Plain text lines

## Install LynxDB

One static binary with no runtime dependencies, for Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64, arm64 and armv7. Apache 2.0 licensed.

[Read the installation guide](https://docs.lynxdb.org/docs/getting-started/install)

```shell
curl -fsSL https://lynxdb.org/install.sh | sh
```

Picks the archive for your architecture and checks it against the release's SHA256SUMS.

```shell
brew install lynxbase/tap/lynxdb
```

One formula per release line too, such as lynxdb@26.11.

```shell
docker run -d -p 3100:3100 \
  -v lynxdb-data:/data \
  ghcr.io/lynxbase/lynxdb server \
  --addr 0.0.0.0:3100 --data-dir /data
```

Images for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. Data stays on the volume.

```shell
go install \
  github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/cmd/lynxdb@main
```

Needs Go 1.26 or later and builds the tip of main.

Check the binary

```console
$ lynxdb version --short
26.11.1.896
```

Stable 26.11.1.896 · 23 November 2026 [All releases](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/releases)

### [Query a log file without a server](https://docs.lynxdb.org/docs/getting-started/pipe-mode)

```console
$ lynxdb query --file app.log \
    'stats count() by level'
```

### [Load a log file into the server](https://docs.lynxdb.org/docs/getting-started/server-mode)

```console
$ lynxdb server
$ lynxdb ingest access.log --index web
```

### [Read the PPL guide](https://docs.lynxdb.org/docs/ppl/overview)

```console
$ lynxdb query \
    'source=web | top 10 uri'
```

## [Twenty-eight bytes from the end: inside the LynxDB engine](https://lynxdb.org/blog/inside-the-lynxdb-engine/)

LynxDB opens a part file from its last 28 bytes, which locate a footer that describes every block: its first sort key, its key runs, its rows per hour. This post follows the Bluesky events from JSON lines into that footer, shows which queries end there and what the design costs, and sets each piece beside ClickHouse's MergeTree.

# Five questions for an access log, answered from the shell

Evgenii Orlov · 27 November 2026 · 4 min read

lynxdb query loads a log file, runs one PPL query over it and exits, with no server to start. We ask a 1,000-line access log where its server errors come from and when they happened.

Something breaks, and the evidence is a log file on a host. This post asks such a file five questions with `lynxdb query`, the pipe mode of [LynxDB](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb): it loads the file, runs one [PPL](https://docs.lynxdb.org/docs/ppl/overview) query over it and prints the result. Every command below was run with LynxDB 26.11.1.896, and every output is what it printed.

## The file

`access.log` is test data from the LynxDB repository[^data]: 1,000 requests to five hosts, one per line, a timestamp followed by `key=value` pairs.

```console
$ head -n 2 access.log
2025-01-15T08:00:00.105Z host=web-03 level=ERROR method=GET path=/api/v1/users status=502 user=grace response_time=786 bytes=32228 msg="GET /api/v1/users completed"
2025-01-15T08:00:00.543Z host=api-02 level=ERROR method=DELETE path=/api/v1/search status=502 user=grace response_time=462 bytes=46701 msg="DELETE /api/v1/search completed"
```

There is no schema to declare. LynxDB reads the timestamp into `_time` and each `key=value` pair into a field when the query runs, so `status` and `response_time` compare as numbers.

## How many events, over what time

```console
$ lynxdb query --file access.log --no-stats \
    'stats count() as events, min(_time) as first, max(_time) as last'
┌────────┬───────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┐
│ events │ first                             │ last                              │
├────────┼───────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
│  1,000 │ 2025-01-15 08:00:00.105 +0000 UTC │ 2025-01-15 08:08:19.524 +0000 UTC │
└────────┴───────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘
(1 row)
```

A thousand events in eight minutes and twenty seconds, from 08:00:00 to 08:08:19 UTC on 15 January 2025.

> **Note:** With `--file`, `lynxdb query` needs no server. It loads the file into a temporary index named `main`, runs the query and exits. A query that names no `source` reads `main`, so the queries in this post start straight with a command.

## Which levels

Without `--no-stats`, the CLI prints a footer under the table: the rows returned, the time the query took and the events it scanned.

```console
$ lynxdb query --file access.log 'stats count() by level'
┌─────────┬───────┐
│ count() │ level │
├─────────┼───────┤
│     294 │ ERROR │
│     359 │ INFO  │
│     347 │ WARN  │
└─────────┴───────┘
(3 rows)
───
  Rows  3
  Took  27ms
  Scanned  1,000
```

The time is from an Apple M4 Pro laptop. The rest of this post passes `--no-stats` to keep the outputs short.

## Where the server errors are

204 of the 1,000 requests ended with a status of 500 or more. Three queries narrow them down.

### By host

`eval` adds a field to every event. Here `error` is 1 for a server error and 0 otherwise, so one `stats` counts the requests and the errors of each host together. A query this long reads better kept in a file, `errors-by-host.ppl`:

```ppl
eval error = if(status >= 500, 1, 0)
| stats count() as requests, sum(error) as errors by host
| eval pct = round(errors * 100.0 / requests, 1)
| sort - pct
```

```console
$ lynxdb query --file access.log --no-stats "$(cat errors-by-host.ppl)"
┌────────┬────────┬──────┬──────────┐
│ host   │ errors │ pct  │ requests │
├────────┼────────┼──────┼──────────┤
│ api-02 │     48 │ 22.6 │      212 │
│ web-02 │     43 │ 22.3 │      193 │
│ web-03 │     41 │ 21.1 │      194 │
│ web-01 │     38 │ 19.7 │      193 │
│ api-01 │     34 │ 16.3 │      208 │
└────────┴────────┴──────┴──────────┘
(5 rows)
```

No host stands out: api-02 fails 22.6% of its requests and api-01, the best, 16.3%.

### Which paths

```console
$ lynxdb query --file access.log --no-stats 'where status >= 500 | top 3 path'
┌───────┬────────────────┐
│ count │ path           │
├───────┼────────────────┤
│    28 │ /api/v1/users  │
│    27 │ /api/v1/orders │
│    25 │ /api/v1/health │
└───────┴────────────────┘
(3 rows)
```

`top` counts the values of a field and keeps the most common. The users, orders and health endpoints lead with 25 to 28 errors each, close together again.

### When

```console
$ lynxdb query --file access.log --no-stats \
    'where status >= 500 | timechart span=1m count()'
┌───────────────────────────────┬─────────┐
│ _time                         │ count() │
├───────────────────────────────┼─────────┤
│ 2025-01-15 08:00:00 +0000 UTC │      20 │
│ 2025-01-15 08:01:00 +0000 UTC │      23 │
│ 2025-01-15 08:02:00 +0000 UTC │      23 │
│ 2025-01-15 08:03:00 +0000 UTC │      25 │
│ 2025-01-15 08:04:00 +0000 UTC │      28 │
│ 2025-01-15 08:05:00 +0000 UTC │      24 │
│ 2025-01-15 08:06:00 +0000 UTC │      26 │
│ 2025-01-15 08:07:00 +0000 UTC │      23 │
│ 2025-01-15 08:08:00 +0000 UTC │      12 │
└───────────────────────────────┴─────────┘
(9 rows)
```

Set against all requests per minute (`timechart span=1m count()` without the `where`), the errors hold steady: 20 to 28 of the 120 requests in every full minute. Nothing spikes, so the cause is not one bad minute.

![Requests per minute in access.log, split into server errors and other statuses](https://lynxdb.org/blog/querying-an-access-log/errors-per-minute.svg)
*Requests per minute in access.log: server errors on the baseline, the other statuses above them. The file ends at 08:08:19, so the last minute holds 40 requests.*

## From standard input

`--file -` reads standard input, so the log can come out of another command: `kubectl logs`, `journalctl` or `ssh` to the host. A result of one value prints as the bare value, ready for a shell variable.

```console
$ cat access.log | lynxdb query --file - --no-stats \
    'where status >= 500 | stats count() as errors'
204
```

The help text puts the whole of pipe mode in three sentences:

> Run a PPL query against a LynxDB server, or with --file against local files. --file - reads standard input. Local input is loaded into the index main, and a local query that names no source reads main.
>
> — `lynxdb query --help`

> **Tip:** When its output goes to a pipe instead of a terminal, `lynxdb query` writes one JSON object per line, ready for `jq`. `--format` (`-F`) picks another format: `table`, `csv`, `tsv`, `markdown`, `json` or `raw`.

## The commands in this post

| PPL command | What it did here |
| --- | --- |
| `stats` | Counted events, overall or per value of a field (`by level`, `by host`) |
| `where` | Kept the events that match a condition (`status >= 500`) |
| `eval` | Added a field to every event, computed from the others |
| `sort` | Ordered the rows; `- pct` sorts by `pct`, highest first |
| `top` | Listed the most common values of a field with their counts |
| `timechart` | Counted events per time bucket (`span=1m`) |

The [PPL guide](https://docs.lynxdb.org/docs/ppl/overview) covers the other commands and every function.

## Keeping the log on a server

Pipe mode reads the file again for every query. To search the same events later, or logs from many hosts, load them into `lynxdb server` and run the same PPL against the stored index:

```shell
# in one terminal
lynxdb server
# in another
lynxdb ingest access.log --index web
lynxdb query 'source=web | where status >= 500 | top 3 path'
```

![The search page of lynxdb server with the query source=web, where status >= 500 and a histogram of the matches](https://lynxdb.org/blog/querying-an-access-log/web-ui.png)
*The Web UI section of lynxdb.org draws the search page of `lynxdb server` on this file: 169 of the 840 events from 08:00 to 08:07 have a status of 500 or more.*

More in the [server mode guide](https://docs.lynxdb.org/docs/getting-started/server-mode).

[^data]: The file is [`testdata/logs/access.log`](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/testdata/logs/access.log) in the LynxDB repository. Clone the repository to run the commands as they are, or point them at a log of your own.


---

Source: https://lynxdb.org/blog/lynxdb-on-jsonbench/

# Fourteen blocks of 61,246: how LynxDB answers JSONBench in 0.18 s

Evgenii Orlov · 27 November 2026 · 17 min read

LynxDB answers JSONBench's five queries over 1 billion Bluesky events in 0.18 s on a warm cache; ClickHouse's published result is 6.9 s. Most of the answer comes from metadata kept per block: the exact distinct count in Q2 opens 14 of 61,246 blocks. Without its sort key LynxDB takes 10.2 s, and ClickHouse is faster.

On 20 November 2026 I ran LynxDB through JSONBench at 1 billion documents on an AWS m6i.8xlarge and posted the totals on LinkedIn: 14 minutes to load, 93 GB on disk, 0.18 s for the five queries. The replies asked for cold times, for what the load time includes, whether the answers match ClickHouse's, and above all what a query reads to come back that fast. The counters the server reports for every query answer most of that, and they also show where the result does not carry over.

> **Note:** Two sets of runs appear below. The published run is commit ad9d7e3b on 20 November: its result files are what the JSONBench page and the LinkedIn post show. The per-query counters (blocks opened, bytes read, memory) come from measurement runs on main 657aa79f on 24 and 25 November, on the same machine type with the same physical design. Their query times agree with the published ones within a few milliseconds. Each number says which run it is from.

Sizes on disk and bytes read are in decimal units (MB, GB); memory is in GiB.

## How JSONBench measures a database

JSONBench is ClickHouse's benchmark for JSON documents, kept in the `json/` directory of the ClickBench repository. Its data is the Bluesky Jetstream feed: 1,000 gzipped files of 1 million JSON lines each, and a dataset of size N is the first N files. At 1 billion the files take 134.1 GB gzipped and 482.1 GB as JSON.

Every system runs on a fresh m6i.8xlarge (32 vCPUs, 128 GB of memory, Ubuntu 24.04, a gp3 volume)[^volume], and the same driver measures it:

1. Install and start the system, then time its `load` script followed by `sync`. That is the load time.
2. Count the documents it holds.
3. For each query: stop the server, drop the page cache, start it again and run the query three times. Run 1 is the cold time; the faster of runs 2 and 3 is the hot time.
4. Read the size on disk after all queries, so merges that finish during the queries count.

The five queries, in PPL as the LynxDB entry runs them:

```ppl
source=bluesky | stats count() as count by commit.collection | sort - count
source=bluesky | where kind = 'commit' and commit.operation = 'create' | stats count() as count, distinct_count(did) as users by commit.collection | sort - count
source=bluesky | where kind = 'commit' and commit.operation = 'create' and commit.collection in ('app.bsky.feed.post', 'app.bsky.feed.repost', 'app.bsky.feed.like') | eval hour_of_day = hour(_time) | stats count() as count by commit.collection, hour_of_day | sort hour_of_day, commit.collection
source=bluesky | where kind = 'commit' and commit.operation = 'create' and commit.collection = 'app.bsky.feed.post' | stats min(_time) as first_post_ts by did | sort first_post_ts | head 3
source=bluesky | where kind = 'commit' and commit.operation = 'create' and commit.collection = 'app.bsky.feed.post' | stats min(_time) as tmin, max(_time) as tmax by did | eval activity_span = timestampdiff(MILLISECOND, from_unixtime(0), tmax) - timestampdiff(MILLISECOND, from_unixtime(0), tmin) | fields did, activity_span | sort - activity_span | head 3
```

| Query | What it asks |
| --- | --- |
| Q1 | Events per collection |
| Q2 | Create events per collection, with the exact number of distinct users |
| Q3 | Post, repost and like creates per collection and UTC hour of day |
| Q4 | The 3 users with the earliest first post |
| Q5 | The 3 users with the longest span between their first and last post |

Each system writes them in its own language. Q2 in ClickHouse SQL and in VictoriaLogs' LogsQL:

```sql
SELECT data.commit.collection AS event, count() AS count, uniqExact(data.did) AS users
FROM bluesky WHERE data.kind = 'commit' AND data.commit.operation = 'create'
GROUP BY event ORDER BY count DESC;
```

```text
{kind=commit,commit.operation=create} | by (commit.collection) count() count, count_uniq(did) users | sort (count desc)
```

The semantics match across LynxDB, ClickHouse and VictoriaLogs: `distinct_count` is exact like `uniqExact`, and `hour(_time)` is the hour in UTC. Elasticsearch and OpenSearch count distinct users approximately, with HyperLogLog++.

### How the LynxDB entry loads and queries

The entry declares its physical design when `load` creates the index, as ClickHouse's script creates its table with `ORDER BY`:

```json
{
  "sort_key": ["kind", "commit.operation", "commit.collection", "did"],
  "time_fields": ["time_us"],
  "partition": "366d"
}
```

Rows are ordered by those four fields and then by time, the same five columns as ClickHouse's `ORDER BY`. One 366-day partition holds every event, as ClickHouse's table has no `PARTITION BY`. LynxDB's own default, daily partitions and no sort key, gets its own section below.

`load` sends 16 files at once, each decompressed with `gzip -dc` and posted with `curl` to `/api/v1/ingest`. It ends with `POST /api/v1/indexes/bluesky/compact`, which returns when the final merge is done, so the load time includes the merges and the queries run with none in flight. In the published run the files took 394 s and the merge 430 s of the 824 s.

`query` is one HTTP request per query, timed by `curl` as the VictoriaLogs entry is:

```shell
curl -sS -G 'http://127.0.0.1:3100/api/v1/query' --data-urlencode "q=${query}"
```

Every response carries what the executor did in `meta.stats`. This is the `meta` of the cold Q2 try in the 25 November measurement run, with the counters that are zero left out:

```json
{
  "took_ms": 54.395,
  "rows": 43,
  "stats": {
    "blocks": 14,
    "skipped_by_key": 3265,
    "counted_by_index": 57967,
    "blocks_matched": 57981,
    "rows_matched": 947048380,
    "held_bytes": 2831000,
    "ordered": true
  }
}
```

Q2 from the command line, with `head 5`, against a server on my laptop (an Apple M4 Pro) that holds the first file of the dataset, 1 million events:

```console
$ lynxdb query --server http://127.0.0.1:3311 \
    'source=bluesky | where kind = "commit" and commit.operation = "create" | stats count() as count, distinct_count(did) as users by commit.collection | sort - count | head 5'
┌───────────────────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ commit.collection     │ count   │ users   │
├───────────────────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ app.bsky.feed.like    │ 444,523 │ 117,617 │
│ app.bsky.graph.follow │ 337,978 │  63,957 │
│ app.bsky.feed.post    │  86,812 │  50,464 │
│ app.bsky.feed.repost  │  56,993 │  26,581 │
│ app.bsky.graph.block  │  13,838 │   5,785 │
└───────────────────────┴─────────┴─────────┘
(5 rows)
───
  Rows  5
  Took  5ms
```

### How the page scores

Per query, the page divides each system's time plus 10 ms by the best time plus 10 ms, and takes the geometric mean of those ratios over the five queries. The combined score weighs that mean for the hot runs at 60%, for the cold runs at 20%, and the load time and the size, each against the best, at 10% each. Lower is better.

The LynxDB entry is not in ClickHouse's repository. It lives in the fork [lynxbase/ClickBench](https://github.com/lynxbase/ClickBench/tree/main/json/lynxdb), and I ran it on my own AWS account in eu-north-1, not in ClickBench's CI. The other systems' rows are the results published in ClickBench.

## One billion events, five systems

**Hot sum of the five queries** (seconds, log scale)

*   LynxDB: 0.18 s
*   ClickHouse: 6.87 s
*   VictoriaLogs: 34.68 s
*   Elasticsearch: 27.09 s
*   OpenSearch: 516.98 s
*   later runs, not on the JSONBench page
*   LynxDB, no key: 10.19 s
*   ClickHouse 26.12: 3.91 s

**Load time** (s, log scale)

*   LynxDB: 824 s
*   ClickHouse: 6,042 s
*   VictoriaLogs: 1,078 s
*   Elasticsearch: 22,255 s
*   OpenSearch: 64,360 s

**Size on disk** (GB)

*   LynxDB: 92.7 GB
*   ClickHouse: 195.8 GB
*   VictoriaLogs: 121.4 GB
*   Elasticsearch: 384.7 GB
*   OpenSearch: 285.1 GB

_JSONBench at 1 billion documents on an AWS m6i.8xlarge. LynxDB is the published run (commit ad9d7e3b, 20 November 2026); the other solid rows are the results published in ClickBench. The outlined rows are later runs on the same machine type: LynxDB at main 657aa79f with its default design and no sort key (25 November), and ClickHouse 26.12.1 rerun by me (24 November)._

| System, version, date | Load | Size | Hot sum | Cold sum | Documents |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LynxDB ad9d7e3b, 2026-11-20 | 824&nbsp;s | 92.7&nbsp;GB | 0.18&nbsp;s | 0.48&nbsp;s | 1,000,000,000 |
| ClickHouse 26.11.1, 2026-11-16 | 6,042&nbsp;s | 195.8&nbsp;GB | 6.87&nbsp;s | 9.24&nbsp;s | 999,999,258 |
| VictoriaLogs v1.53.0, 2026-11-02 | 1,078&nbsp;s | 121.4&nbsp;GB | 34.68&nbsp;s | 40.22&nbsp;s | 999,999,241 |
| Elasticsearch 9.5.6, 2026-11-02 | 22,255&nbsp;s | 384.7&nbsp;GB | 27.09&nbsp;s | 27.35&nbsp;s | 999,999,034 |
| OpenSearch 3.9.0, 2026-11-04 | 64,360&nbsp;s | 285.1&nbsp;GB | 516.98&nbsp;s | 202.13&nbsp;s | 999,999,241 |

The hot times per query, in seconds:

| Query | LynxDB | ClickHouse | VictoriaLogs | Elasticsearch | OpenSearch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Q1 | 0.0012 | 0.239 | 0.033 | 0.618 | 19.922 |
| Q2 | 0.049 | 2.767 | 19.155 | 4.930 | 59.570 |
| Q3 | 0.062 | 2.302 | 1.521 | 14.213 | 412.161 |
| Q4 | 0.0028 | 0.757 | 5.914 | 3.443 | 6.960 |
| Q5 | 0.063 | 0.805 | 8.053 | 3.887 | 18.367 |

Cold, the published run took 1.8, 49.7, 103.3, 8.0 and 319.8 ms for Q1 to Q5. Q5 makes up 257 of the 305 ms between the cold and hot sums, because it is the only query that reads much column data.

The page's combined score puts ClickHouse at 19.03 times LynxDB's, VictoriaLogs at 29.55, Elasticsearch at 65.2 and OpenSearch at 399.7 (my replication of the page's code). The ratio grows with the data: ClickHouse's is 1.89 at 1 million documents and 7.25 at 100 million.

OpenSearch's Q3 is slower hot than cold (412 s against 91 s), which inflates its hot sum; Elasticsearch's Q3 does the same (14.2 s against 5.9 s).

## The sort key decides what each query reads

In the measurement run the 1B store holds 92 parts with 61,246 blocks of up to 16,384 rows. Besides the column data, each part ends in a footer that describes its blocks:

- the first sort key of every block, its row count and its time range;
- for every block, how many distinct key prefixes it holds at each depth of the sort key (`KeyRuns`), and how many leading key columns its first row shares with the last row of the block before (`KeyShared`);
- exact value counts for string fields with at most 256 values;
- row counts per UTC minute, hour and day for every block.

Next to the column data, each block also has token filters for its string columns. When the server starts it reads 151 MiB (158 MB) in 1.39 s. About 34 MB of that is its own executable, which it loads into the page cache before it listens; the rest is the part footers, which opening the index reads. The benchmark's `check` passes only after that, so no query pays for the read. The ClickHouse entry also loads its primary keys at startup. How the footer is laid out and built is the subject of the next post, [Inside the LynxDB engine](https://lynxdb.org/blog/inside-the-lynxdb-engine/).

With the benchmark's sort key, four of the five queries find most of their answer in that metadata.

**Where each answer comes from** (sort key: kind, operation, collection, did)

blocks read

**Part footers, in memory read when the server starts**

Q1 events per collection → Value counts: commit.collection, per part → 0

Q2 creates and users → Key runs: KeyRuns, KeyShared per block → 14

Q3 creates by hour → Hour buckets: rows per UTC hour, per block → 5

**Column data, on disk**

Q4 first posters → Time-ordered scan with a bound: stops past the 3rd first post → 32

Q5 longest activity → Run ends from \_time: first and last row per did → 5,513

* * *

Q2 Q3 Q5 no sort key → Hash aggregation over every block: Q1 and Q4 keep their paths → 61,041

_The path each query takes on the 1B store, and the number of blocks whose rows were read on the cold try. Counts from the measurement run on main 657aa79f (25 November 2026): 61,246 blocks with the sort key, 61,043 without it._

### Q1 sums value counts from 92 footers

Q1 has no filter and groups by `commit.collection`, a field with a few dozen values. Every part's footer already holds the exact count of each value, so the executor adds up 92 small tables and opens no block. The cold try read 0.07 MB and took 1.9 ms, with or without the sort key.

### Q2 counts distinct users from key runs

Q2 filters on the first two key columns, groups by the third and counts distinct values of the fourth. In key order, the rows of one user sit next to each other inside a collection, so the number of distinct users in a collection is the number of `did` runs in it.

The footer stores those runs per block. If a block holds one collection (`KeyRuns` at depth 3 is 1), the executor adds the block's row count to the collection's count and its `KeyRuns` at depth 4 to the users, less one when the block's first row continues the previous block's last user (`KeyShared` of 4). Only blocks in which the collection changes have to be opened.

**Q2 on 61,246 blocks in sort-key order** (schematic)

**the 61,246 blocks to scale**

*   skipped by key **3,265**
*   counted from key runs **57,967**
*   opened **14**

**A block inside one collection**: KeyRuns(3) = 1; count += rows; users += KeyRuns(4); users -= 1 if KeyShared ≥ 4

**A block where the collection changes**: KeyRuns(3) > 1; opened, and its rows grouped as they are read

_Q2's path through the 1B store. Blocks outside `kind = commit` , `operation = create` are skipped by their first keys; blocks that hold one collection are counted from the footer; blocks where a collection changes are opened. The strip is a schematic, one square for many blocks; the share bar and the counts are from the cold Q2 try of the measurement run (main 657aa79f, 25 November 2026)._

Most of the 43 collections with create events are tiny and share blocks, so 14 blocks hold every collection boundary. The cold try read 1.9 MB (1.4 MB in two repeats), used 0.20 CPU-seconds and peaked at 190 MiB, for 0.056 s cold and 0.053 s hot (0.050 and 0.049 s in the published run).

The count is exact as long as the parts follow one another in key order, so that a user's runs never sit in two places; after the final merge they do. With daily partitions and the same key the store has 488 parts in several key-ordered streams, and Q2 counts 63,003 blocks from another per-block record (`counted_by_entries`), opens 1,090, reads 1.5 GB and takes 2.77 s cold and 1.05 s hot.

### Q3 counts from hour buckets

The hour of day is not in the sort key, so Q3 uses the time buckets: a block that holds a single collection, all of it `commit` and `create`, contributes its row counts per UTC hour straight from the footer.

Key ranges from the `in` list skip 21,796 blocks and the token filters 1,922. Of the remaining 37,528, the executor counts 37,523 from their hour records and reads rows from 5, so the `blocks` counter says 37,528 while the device read 0.5 MB. Walking those records still costs 1.34 CPU-seconds; the cold try took 0.099 s (0.103 s in the published run).

### Q4 scans in time order and stops early

Q4 asks for the three smallest `min(_time)` per user among post creates. The planner turns `sort | head 3` into a top-3, and the executor visits blocks in order of their earliest row. Once it has three users, it skips every block whose earliest row is later than the third of them: such a block cannot hold a smaller first post.

It opened 32 blocks, read 3.2 MB and took 7.1 ms cold. The rest were skipped: 3,686 by key, 5,481 by time, and 52,047 under the token counter, which I read as whole parts with no `app.bsky.feed.post` in their footer value counts. Q4 does not need the key either: on the store without one it opens a single block.

### Q5 is the query that reads data

Q5 needs the first and last post of each of 3.9 million users, 89.9 million rows. In key order a user's posts are one run sorted by time, so the executor reads the `_time` column of the 5,513 blocks of post creates and takes the ends of each run, with no hash table.

That is 518 MB from the device, 1.5 CPU-seconds and 734 MiB of peak memory, for 0.317 s cold and 0.063 s hot[^q5].

## Without the sort key, ClickHouse is faster

LynxDB's default design, daily partitions and no sort key, loads the 1B dataset in 1,008 s into 107.8 GB and runs the five queries in 10.19 s hot and 34.95 s cold (main 657aa79f, 25 November). ClickHouse 26.11's published sums are 6.87 s and 9.24 s.

**The cold try with and without the sort key** (MB read (log scale), blocks read, time)

*   **Q1** events per collection
*   sort key: 0.07 MB (0 blocks · 0.0019 s)
*   no key: 0.07 MB (0 blocks · 0.0019 s)
*   **Q2** creates and users
*   sort key: 1.9 MB (14 blocks · 0.056 s)
*   no key: 11,792 MB (61,041 blocks · 13.43 s)
*   **Q3** creates by hour
*   sort key: 0.5 MB (5 blocks · 0.099 s)
*   no key: 3,530 MB (61,041 blocks · 9.31 s)
*   **Q4** first posters
*   sort key: 3.2 MB (32 blocks · 0.0071 s)
*   no key: 0.17 MB (1 block · 0.0109 s)
*   **Q5** longest activity
*   sort key: 518 MB (5,513 blocks · 0.317 s)
*   no key: 13,755 MB (61,041 blocks · 12.13 s)

_Bytes read from the device on the cold try of each query, the blocks whose rows were read (with the key, Q3 also counts 37,523 blocks from their hour buckets) and the cold time. 1B store on an m6i.8xlarge, main 657aa79f, 25 November 2026: with the sort key in one partition (61,246 blocks), and in LynxDB's default design of daily partitions without a key (61,043 blocks)._

Q1 and Q4 keep their paths. Q2, Q3 and Q5 read every block and group rows in hash tables: Q2 reads 11.8 GB, uses 137 CPU-seconds and peaks at 14.5 GiB, for 13.43 s cold and 5.17 s hot, and Q5 takes 12.13 s cold and 3.91 s hot.

Daily partitions with the sort key sit between the two at 1.35 s hot, most of it Q2, which loses the key-run count across partitions.

### Memory on the hash path

The hash aggregation behind the no-key numbers changed after the published run. Until 24 November each scan goroutine kept a private log of its groups and distinct values until the scan ended, so memory grew with the number of rows. Commit 8655937b, merged that day, stages them under one shared budget of 1 GiB (and as much again for distinct values) and drains them into hash partitions that all goroutines share.

**Peak memory of the server on the cold try** (GiB, no sort key)

*   **top accounts** stats count() by did | sort - n | head 10
*   before: 38.71
*   after: 13.48
*   **Q2** creates and users
*   before: 25.12
*   after: 14.50
*   **distinct accounts** stats distinct\_count(did)
*   before: 23.23
*   after: 12.90
*   **Q5** longest activity
*   before: 19.54
*   after: 15.73

_Peak memory of the server (VmHWM) on the cold try, 1B store without a sort key (daily partitions, 107.8 GB), m6i.8xlarge, 24 November 2026: main 400bddbb before the change, 8655937b after._

Times moved little: Q2 went from 14.38 s to 13.48 s cold. Built with a very large budget, the same commit went back to 37.38 GiB for top accounts, so the budget is what cuts the memory. The sort-key design builds no such tables for Q2 to Q5.

## Where the sort key helps and where it works against it

Five queries are a narrow test, so I also wrote 25 log-style queries and ran all 30 cold and hot at 1B on the same machine type: LynxDB on the benchmark's design (main 657aa79f, 25 November), ClickHouse 26.12.1 and VictoriaLogs v1.54.0 (24 November). LynxDB is faster than both on 21 of the 30 cold and 19 of the 30 hot, and it does so from the smallest store of the five systems: 92.7 GB against 121.4 to 384.7 GB.

**LynxDB against the faster of ClickHouse and VictoriaLogs** (cold time ratio, log scale)

    Events that reply to another post, counted per UTC hour of day. LynxDB read rows from 61,246 of 61,246 blocks on the cold try.
    
    ```
    source=bluesky | where isnotnull(commit.record.reply.parent.uri) | eval hour_of_day = hour(_time) | stats count() as n by hour_of_day | sort hour_of_day
    ```
    
    | Time | cold | hot |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | LynxDB | 6.79 s | 0.629 s |
    | ClickHouse | 1.02 s | 0.443 s |
    | VictoriaLogs | 0.488 s | 0.356 s |
    
*   latest 100 in 5 minutes **14×**
    
    The 100 most recent events in that 5-minute window. LynxDB read rows from 58,553 of 61,246 blocks on the cold try.
    
    ```
    source=bluesky earliest='2024-11-28 12:00:00' latest='2024-11-28 12:05:00' | sort - _time | head 100
    ```
    
    | Time | cold | hot |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | LynxDB | 3.62 s | 0.223 s |
    | ClickHouse | 3.52 s | 0.0390 s |
    | VictoriaLogs | 0.257 s | 0.0741 s |
    
*   a word within 1 hour **22×**
    
    Counts events with 'love' in the post text from 12:00 to 13:00 on 28 November 2024. LynxDB read rows from 5,478 of 61,246 blocks on the cold try.
    
    ```
    source=bluesky earliest='2024-11-28 12:00:00' latest='2024-11-28 13:00:00' | where match(commit.record.text, 'love') | stats count() as n
    ```
    
    | Time | cold | hot |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | LynxDB | 3.17 s | 0.507 s |
    | ClickHouse | 3.54 s | 0.0710 s |
    | VictoriaLogs | 0.142 s | 0.0686 s |
    
*   count in a 5-minute window **73×**
    
    Counts events per collection from 12:00 to 12:05 on 28 November 2024. LynxDB read rows from 30 of 61,246 blocks on the cold try.
    
    ```
    source=bluesky earliest='2024-11-28 12:00:00' latest='2024-11-28 12:05:00' | stats count() as n by commit.collection
    ```
    
    | Time | cold | hot |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | LynxDB | 3.48 s | 0.151 s |
    | ClickHouse | 3.39 s | 0.0360 s |
    | VictoriaLogs | 0.0479 s | 0.0060 s |
    
*   **No time to compare, 0** no hot run on ClickHouse

_LynxDB's time divided by the time of the faster of ClickHouse and VictoriaLogs (or of the one chosen), for the five JSONBench queries and 25 log queries at 1B on an m6i.8xlarge. Cold is the first run after a restart with the page cache dropped, hot the faster of runs 2 and 3. LynxDB: main 657aa79f with the benchmark's sort key in one partition (25 November 2026). ClickHouse 26.12.1 and VictoriaLogs v1.54.0: 24 November 2026. ClickHouse has no hot time for the query over any field: its one cold run took 591 s._

The 15 clear wins are the queries where the sort key, the footer or a token filter rules out most blocks before a row is read. Besides the five JSONBench queries:

- A word in any field (`source=bluesky earthquake | stats count()`) takes 0.88 s cold, against 98.4 s for VictoriaLogs and 591 s for ClickHouse. The token filters skip 58,391 of the 61,246 blocks.
- The latest 100 events take 0.098 s, against 0.37 s and 3.58 s. The block time ranges in the footer leave 128 blocks to read.
- One record by its key (`commit.rkey="3lbhuei4dic2u"`) takes 0.17 s, against 1.12 s and 5.47 s, from 71 blocks.

Six more come out within 11% of the faster rival: the five that read all post text (a common word, a phrase, a substring, a regular expression and the length of the text, about 2.75 s against ClickHouse's 3.05 s) and the first 100 events.

The nine losses come from the same sort key. Rows are ordered by kind, operation, collection and user before time, so a time window is spread over almost every block of the one long partition: counting events per collection in a 5-minute window skips only 2,691 blocks by time, reads 4.7 GB and takes 3.48 s cold, against VictoriaLogs' 0.048 s. LynxDB's default design, daily partitions without a key, counts the same window in 0.0064 s, and loses JSONBench instead.

A field outside the key and present in few events is the other weak spot: replies per hour (a field in 4.5% of events) reads all 61,246 blocks, 6.79 s against VictoriaLogs' 0.49 s. Top and distinct accounts (2.74 and 2.72 s against ClickHouse's 1.46 and 1.12 s) group by `did` across every collection, and the latest 100 posts containing a common word need the time order that the key does not give (1.33 s against 0.90 s). Some ClickHouse hot times may also benefit from its query condition cache; I have not checked.

Text search shows the same trade-off between the two LynxDB designs. The key packs the post text into about 5,500 blocks of 16,384 posts each, while without it posts are under one row in ten of every block. A rare word (`match(commit.record.text, 'earthquake')`) opens 2,273 blocks with the key and 7,744 without, but reads 1.6 GB against 0.7 GB and takes 0.56 s cold against 0.36 s. A regular expression gets no help from token filters: 2.76 s cold and 0.36 s hot with the key, 4.08 s and 0.14 s without.

On the five JSONBench queries alone, ClickHouse 26.12.1, which the ClickHouse entry's scripts installed when I reran it on 24 November, sums 3.91 s hot and 5.32 s cold, against 6.87 s and 9.24 s for the published 26.11: faster than LynxDB without a sort key, slower than LynxDB with one.

The load scripts differ as well. LynxDB's loads 16 files at once, VictoriaLogs' 8, and ClickHouse's one file per `INSERT`, one after another; LynxDB also waits for its final merge inside the load time. The load-time ratio says as much about the scripts as about the engines.

## What the JSONBench page shows and hides

LynxDB stores nested objects as columns named by their dotted paths and returns events flat: `{"a": {"b": 1}}` and `{"a.b": 1}` come back the same, while arrays, empty objects and nulls are kept. Its `retains_structure` is therefore `no`, and the JSONBench page's Flattening filter leaves such systems out by default. In that default view ClickHouse leads at 1B.

The page also scores the size of each entry's scripts after `zstd -19`. LynxDB's is 1,954 bytes, against ClickHouse 746, VictoriaLogs 1,331, OpenSearch 3,023 and Elasticsearch 3,538, which ranks it 20th of 29. At the smaller sizes Opteryx loads faster (1M to 100M), and CLP is smaller at 1M and 10M.

The dataset has 759 lines that LynxDB does not load as documents: 755 are not JSON objects (documents longer than 64 KiB split over two lines), and 4 are objects in file_0178 whose `commit.record.langs` is nested 2,163 levels deep, beyond LynxDB's limit of 256. The published run kept all 759 as text events, so it counts 1,000,000,000 lines and scores 100% data quality, where ClickHouse loads 999,999,258 and VictoriaLogs 999,999,241. Since 23 November `/api/v1/ingest` refuses such lines, and main holds 999,999,241 events, as many as VictoriaLogs.

The entry's README states that the answers match ClickHouse's at 10M and 100M, apart from the row of the non-JSON lines. At 1B I compared the stored answers of main 657aa79f (25 November) with those of ClickHouse 26.12. Q3, Q4 and Q5 are identical. Q2 differs in one row: `app.bsky.labeler.service` has 188 events and 117 users against 189 and 118. Q1 differs in two: `app.bsky.graph.list` 276,933 against 276,948 and `app.bsky.labeler.service` 1,757 against 1,759. The 17 events are exactly the difference between the documents the two systems loaded; I have not traced which documents they are.

## Why ClickHouse's table is twice the size

LynxDB stores each field once, as its own column, and keeps no copy of the raw JSON: 92.7 GB for a billion documents is 92.7 bytes each, against 482 bytes of JSON. In the measurement run's store, token filters take 7.9 GB of 91.9 GB.

ClickHouse's table is about LynxDB's size at 1M and 10M documents (1.01 and 1.03 times) and twice it from 100M (2.05) to 1B (2.11). Its schema uses the JSON type with the `advanced` serialization for shared data, and ClickHouse's blog says that since 25.8 this format stores "a copy of the data in the original format alongside the advanced one", which "effectively doubles the storage requirement"[^ch]. My sampling of the 26.11 table agrees with that: fresh parts take 94 to 102 bytes per row and merged parts 191 to 199, both with ZSTD(3). The blog does not say the copy is tied to merged parts; that link is my reading of the sample.

## What I have not measured

- Queries while ingest and merges run. Before the final merge the parts overlap in key range, so Q2 would most likely take the multi-stream path shown above for daily partitions; I have no numbers for it.
- A ClickHouse projection or materialized view. One would likely do Q2's work at write time; neither side uses them in this benchmark.
- ClickHouse loaded in parallel, as LynxDB is.
- The answers of the published build ad9d7e3b at 1B.

The result files, the scripts and the README are in [lynxbase/ClickBench](https://github.com/lynxbase/ClickBench/tree/main/json/lynxdb); `./benchmark.sh` in `json/lynxdb` runs the entry through the shared JSONBench driver. If the method has a flaw, tell me and I will rerun it. The next post, [Inside the LynxDB engine](https://lynxdb.org/blog/inside-the-lynxdb-engine/), opens the part file: the footer, the key runs, the time buckets and the hash path.

[^volume]: JSONBench's standard volume is 2,000 GB of gp3 at 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MB/s. The volume of LynxDB's published run was not recorded; the measurement runs used 1,000 GB at 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s.
[^q5]: Q5's counters account for 61,218 of the 61,246 blocks: 5,513 opened and 55,705 skipped by key. The other 28 are not reported by any counter.
[^ch]: [JSON data type gets even better](https://clickhouse.com/blog/json-data-type-gets-even-better), ClickHouse blog.


---

Source: https://lynxdb.org/blog/inside-the-lynxdb-engine/

# Twenty-eight bytes from the end: inside the LynxDB engine

Evgenii Orlov · 27 November 2026 · 16 min read

LynxDB opens a part file from its last 28 bytes, which locate a footer that describes every block: its first sort key, its key runs, its rows per hour. This post follows the Bluesky events from JSON lines into that footer, shows which queries end there and what the design costs, and sets each piece beside ClickHouse's MergeTree.

[The previous post](https://lynxdb.org/blog/lynxdb-on-jsonbench/) counted what each JSONBench query reads from a billion Bluesky events. This one opens the files behind those counts and sets them beside ClickHouse's MergeTree. Mechanisms are as the code has them at commit 314ce56f (25 November 2026). Numbers at 1 billion events come from the previous post's measurement runs (main 657aa79f, m6i.8xlarge, 24 and 25 November); a few come from a store of the first million events on my laptop, an Apple M4 Pro, and say so. Sizes on disk and bytes read are in decimal units; memory is in GiB.

## From an index to a column chunk

LynxDB keeps an index as six levels in one directory. The index (`bluesky`) fixes its sort key, time fields and partition width when it is created. A partition is a fixed span of event time, a UTC day by default; merges stay inside one and retention drops whole ones. The JSONBench entry asks for 366 days, so one partition holds the dataset. A run is one sorted sequence of rows in a partition: each flush writes one run per partition it touches, and runs overlap in key and time until they are merged. A part is one file holding a contiguous key range of a run. A block holds up to 16,384 rows, and a column chunk holds the values of one path of one kind in a block, so a path that arrives with two types gets two chunks. After the final merge the 1B store is one run of 92 parts and 61,246 blocks, about 16,300 rows each.

ClickHouse's MergeTree has one level fewer. Each part of a table is sorted by the `ORDER BY` key on its own, and background merges combine the parts of a partition into larger ones ([parts](https://clickhouse.com/docs/parts)). A part is a directory, with a data file and a marks file per column in the Wide format. Its rows fall into granules of at most `index_granularity` rows, 8,192 by default, the smallest set of rows ClickHouse reads ([MergeTree](https://clickhouse.com/docs/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/mergetree)).

**From an index to a column chunk** (the 1B store beside a MergeTree table)

LynxDB, counts at 1B

ClickHouse MergeTree

**Index**: sort key, time fields, partition width

**Table**: ORDER BY five columns, one JSON column

**Partition1**: a span of event time, 366 days here

**Partition**: any PARTITION BY expression, none here

**Run1**: one sorted sequence of rows

**No run**: each part is sorted on its own

**Part file92**: a key range of a run, one file

**Part**: a directory, files per column

**Block61,246**: up to 16,384 rows

**Granule**: up to 8,192 rows, one mark

**Column chunk**: one path and kind in a block

**Column data**: the granule's rows in the column's .bin, found by its mark

_The levels of LynxDB's 1B store beside those of a MergeTree table. LynxDB's counts are from the measurement run on main 657aa79f (25 November 2026); ClickHouse's levels follow its MergeTree documentation, and its table is the JSONBench entry's._

## The part file, front to back

The writer emits a part in one pass ([part/format.go](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/pkg/colstore/part/format.go)). An 8-byte header holds the magic `LXPT` and the format version. The blocks follow, each a sequence of column chunks, with the token filters of every group of up to 128 blocks behind the group's last block. Then come the column directories of all blocks, the footer, and a 28-byte trailer: the footer's offset, length and CRC-32C, the version and the magic again[^dict]. A directory has a 28-byte entry per chunk (path, kind, encoding, number of values, place in the file, checksum), followed by numeric bounds and a constant where the chunk has one. The footer describes every block without touching its data.

**A part file, front to back** (byte ranges in file order, not to scale)

header8 B _at open_ block 0: column chunks _when a query opens it_ block 1: column chunks _when a query opens it_ up to 128 blocks a group token-filter pages of the group _page by page, per probe_ more groups column directories, one per block _on a block's first open_ footer _at open, kept in memory_ trailer28 B _at open, read first_

**The footer's records** (bytes in the 1M store)

**Paths**: names, sort key; 12,081 B

**Block index**: 52 B a block: rows, time bounds, offsets; 3,915 B

**Filter entries**: 16 B a filter, 20 B a group; 9,662 B

**First keys**: a block's first key, the part's last; 6,815 B

**Key statistics**: KeyShared, KeyRuns per depth; 449 B

**Totals**: rows, bytes, time bounds; 465 B

**Value counts**: string paths of up to 256 values; 323,884 B

**Time buckets**: rows per minute, hour, day; 5,275 B

_A part's byte ranges in file order, when the server reads each, and the records of the footer. Sizes are from the store of the first million events on my laptop (15 parts, 75 blocks, read with build 7c88422e): column chunks take 91.0% of its 98.2 MB, token-filter pages 8.6%, footers 0.37% and directories 0.06%._

`GET /api/v1/indexes/{index}/columns` reports how an index's bytes divide over these regions. For the footers of the 1M store, served on my laptop:

```console
$ curl -s 127.0.0.1:3331/api/v1/indexes/bluesky/columns \
    | jq -r '.data.breakdown[] | select(.name|test("^footer")) | "\(.name) \(.bytes)"' \
    | column -t
footer.counted_values  323884
footer.paths           12006
footer.filter_entries  9262
footer.block_keys      6815
footer.time_counts     5275
footer.block_index     3915
footer.totals          465
footer.key_stats       449
footer.filter_groups   400
footer.sort_key        75
```

A reader opens a part from its end: it reads the trailer, checks the footer's checksum and validates its records, for instance that each block's time buckets add up to its rows. The server maps every file twice ([dir.go](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/pkg/colstore/dir.go)), with the kernel's read-ahead for the footer and directories and with random access for chunks and filter pages. It copies the block index, filter entries, time buckets and first keys onto the heap, so finding a block reads no page of the file. A block's directory is copied when a query first opens the block; chunks and filter pages are read when a query needs them and checked against their own checksums.

On the 1B store the server reads 151 MiB from the device in 1.39 s while it starts. About 34 MB of that is its own executable, which it reads into the page cache before it listens; the rest is what opening the 92 parts reads: their footers, and no column data. The benchmark's `check` passes only after that, so no query pays for it.

ClickHouse keeps the same pieces in separate files of a part's directory ([sparse primary indexes](https://clickhouse.com/docs/guides/best-practices/sparse-primary-indexes)). `primary.idx` holds one mark per granule, the key of its first row, and is meant to stay in memory; the ClickHouse entry loads it at startup. A marks file per column locates each granule's compressed block in the column's `.bin` file and its offset once decompressed, and in `.mrk2` files its row count. LynxDB's first keys play the part of `primary.idx` and its directories that of the marks, except that a directory entry also carries the chunk's value count, bounds and constant, which ClickHouse keeps per granule only in a declared `minmax` skip index.

## Key runs let Q2 count without opening blocks

For every block the writer stores two records about the sort key ([part/writer.go](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/pkg/colstore/part/writer.go)). `KeyShared` is the number of leading key columns that the block's first row shares with the row before it. `KeyRuns` at depth d is the number of distinct values that the first d key columns take in the block. The writer finds, for each row, the first key column that differs from the row before; `KeyRuns(d)` is one plus the number of rows that differ within the first d columns. With four key columns that is five varints a block, 449 bytes for the 75 blocks of the 1M store.

**Key runs in three blocks of one part** (sort key: kind, operation, collection, did)

**Block 1**: likes; rows 16,384; KeyShared 3; KeyRuns 1 1 1 4,286; count += 16,384 users += 4,286

**Block 2**: likes, then posts; rows 16,384; KeyShared 3; KeyRuns 1 1 2 4,385; opened: the collection changes

**Block 3**: posts; rows 16,384; KeyShared 4; KeyRuns 1 1 1 9,764; count += 16,384 users += 9,763

*   counted from the footer
*   opened, rows read

_Three consecutive blocks of one part of the 1M store, with the values their footer holds, and what Q2 does with each. Block 3's first row continues the last user of block 2 (KeyShared 4), so it adds one user fewer than its KeyRuns at depth 4._

Q2 counts a block that lies inside `commit`, `create` and holds one collection from these records alone, as the previous post showed ([exec/agg_ordered.go](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/pkg/colstore/exec/agg_ordered.go)). The first block of a part stores `KeyShared` 0; for it the reader compares the block's first key with the last key of the part before it, which that part's footer keeps. A flush cuts its run between keys, so no user spans two of its parts: in the 1M store each part's first row shares three key columns with the previous part's last row, never four.

In the 1M store these records predict Q2's counters exactly. Seven blocks hold a key change inside the range or cross its end and must be opened, three lie outside it, and the other 65 are counted, which is what the query reports.

The count is exact only within one key-ordered stream, so the planner takes this path only when the key ranges form one. While overlapping runs wait to be merged, or with daily partitions, a block inside one collection contributes the entries of its `did` dictionary instead, read without the rest of the block (`counted_by_entries`). On daily partitions with the same key, Q2 counted 63,003 blocks that way and opened 1,090, and took 2.77 s cold against 0.056 s.

ClickHouse's sparse index holds the key of each granule's first row and nothing about what lies between. It finds where `commit`, `create` begins and ends, and, as I understand it, `uniqExact` then reads `did` for every matching row. ClickHouse would do this work at write time instead, with a projection that has a `GROUP BY`, stored in each part as a hidden AggregatingMergeTree part ([projections](https://clickhouse.com/docs/data-modeling/projections)); the entry defines none.

## Time buckets per minute, hour and day

Every block also counts its rows per UTC minute, hour and day ([part/timecounts.go](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/pkg/colstore/part/timecounts.go)). The writer counts the rows once, in the narrowest width whose span stays under 65,536 buckets, and adds those up for the wider widths. It keeps a record only if the record fits in 4 KiB, about two bytes a bucket, which holds a day of minutes, and stores the records widest first.

A query uses them when it counts rows by `hour(_time)` or `bin(_time, w)`, alone or with columns that hold one value throughout the block ([exec/agg_time.go](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/pkg/colstore/exec/agg_time.go)). The executor picks the widest record whose width divides the time keys' widths, hours for `hour(_time)` and minutes for a 5-minute bin, and under a plain time range the narrowest. The block's directory must settle every other predicate for all its rows, or the block is counted row by row and the reason goes to a `time_missed_*` counter. Q3 at 1B counted 37,523 blocks from hour records and missed 5.

The dataset's events run from 21 November to 4 December 2024. In key order a block holds a slice of accounts with all their events, so most blocks span the twelve days: their minute records outgrow 4 KiB and are dropped, and their time bounds overlap any window. A 5-minute count therefore took 3.48 s cold on this design, reading 4.7 GB, against 0.0064 s on daily partitions without a key. VictoriaLogs keeps daily partitions ([key concepts](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victorialogs/keyconcepts/)) and a sparse index of timestamps, and stores each stream's logs together ([FAQ](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victorialogs/faq/)); it answered the window in 0.048 s.

## What rules a block out before it is opened

The scan ([scan.go](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/pkg/colstore/scan.go)) applies its rules in a fixed order. Per part: its time bounds, then the footer's value counts, which drop a part that lacks the string of an equality such as `commit.collection = 'app.bsky.feed.post'`, then a binary search of the first keys for the key prefix or the ranges of an `in` list. Per block: its time bounds, a cache of blocks that an earlier query with the same condition found empty, and the token filters. An opened block can still be rejected by its directory before any chunk is decoded. Each rule has its counter in `meta.stats`:

| Counter | Decided by | Cold, 1B, sort key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `skipped_by_time` | part and block time bounds | Q4: 5,481 |
| `skipped_by_key` | first keys | Q2: 3,265 |
| `skipped_by_token` | footer value counts, token filters | rare word: 58,973 |
| `skipped_as_empty` | blocks an earlier query found empty | 0 on every cold try |
| `skipped_by_stats` | an opened block's directory | regular expression: 55,471 |
| `counted_by_index` | footer value counts, key runs | Q2: 57,967 |
| `counted_by_time` | time buckets | Q3: 37,523 |

A part dropped by its value counts is booked under the token counter; as far as I can tell, that is where most of Q4's 52,047 token skips come from.

Token filters are the one per-block structure kept outside the footer ([tokenfilter/cells.go](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/pkg/colstore/tokenfilter/cells.go)). The writer hashes every token, a maximal run of letters and digits, case-folded, to 64 bits. A column whose encoded chunk reaches 16 KiB gets a filter of its own, so that a search can tell which columns to read; the block's smaller columns share one. A filter splits its hashes into cells by their high bits and keeps each cell as a sorted set of shortened hashes coded after Elias and Fano, aiming at one false positive in 800 probes for a column's own filter and one in 200 for the shared one. A group's filters are stored in stripes, so that probing one token across the group reads one stripe of at most 48 KiB, in 4 KiB pages with their own checksums. On the 1B store they take 7.88 GB of 91.88 GB, 8.6%.

In ClickHouse such filters are opt-in. A data-skipping index is declared per expression, summarizes `GRANULARITY` granules, and comes as `minmax`, `set`, `bloom_filter`, the deprecated `tokenbf_v1`, or a `text` index, an inverted index that is generally available from 26.2 ([skipping indexes](https://clickhouse.com/docs/optimize/skipping-indexes)). The JSONBench entry declares none. VictoriaLogs, like LynxDB, writes bloom filters for every block, to skip blocks without a given word.

## Ingest: from a JSON line to a merged part

The entry's load script decompresses 16 files at once and posts each as one request. The server reads a request's body on one goroutine and parses it on another ([rest/ingest.go](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/pkg/api/rest/ingest.go)), into the first free one of the store's append buffers, one per CPU. The 16 requests parse in parallel; by my reading of the code, one request does not spread over more cores.

The parser writes JSON straight into typed column builders, with no document tree in between ([shred/parse.go](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/pkg/colstore/shred/parse.go)). A nested member becomes its dotted path, and each value goes to the column of its kind there, so a field that is a string in one event and a number in the next gets two columns, and an explicit `null` stays apart from a missing field. Arrays, empty objects and objects nested deeper than 64 levels are kept whole in a binary variant column; past 256 levels the line is refused, which keeps out 4 objects of the dataset nested 2,163 levels deep. Members beyond a batch's 8,192 columns go into one variant object, `_rest`. Nothing keeps the original line.

A flush starts when a buffer has waited a second, when buffered input reaches its budget, or on a sync. Up to two run at once, each sorting its batches by partition and key on half the CPUs, cutting the run into parts of disjoint key ranges and writing them in parallel at zstd's fastest level ([store_run.go](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/pkg/colstore/store_run.go)). Each chunk takes the encoding that suits it, among them a constant, a sorted dictionary of up to 65,536 values with row counts per value when there are at most 256, numeric differences for strings such as time-ordered IDs, and presence alone.

Merges are tiered: the eight oldest runs of a tier become one run of the next, and at most 64 runs may wait ([store.go](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/pkg/colstore/store.go)). A merge re-encodes the blocks of flushed runs at zstd's default level, copies other blocks unchanged where the key order allows, and splits large ranges among workers under a shared budget of decoded blocks. The load ends by compacting the partition into one run.

**From 16 gzip streams to 92 parts** (the entry's load at 1B)

**Load script16 streams**: gzip -dc | curl, one request per file

server, in memory

**Request2 goroutines**: the body read on one, parsed on the other

**Shred**: JSON into typed column builders by dotted path

**Append buffers32**: one per CPU, the first free one taken

server, on disk

**Flushtier 0**: sort by partition and key, cut by key range, zstd fastest

**Tiered merges15,022 parts, 99.23 GB**: 8 runs of a tier into 1, zstd default

**Compact92 parts, 91.88 GB**: every run of the partition into one

_The path of an event from the entry's load script to a merged part. Part counts and sizes are from the measurement run on main 657aa79f (25 November 2026), where the load took 803.5 s, 402.8 s of it in the final compaction; the published run took 824 s, 430 s of it merging._

The ClickHouse entry inserts one file at a time with `FORMAT JSONAsObject`. A JSON column keeps the typed paths its type declares as columns, up to `max_dynamic_paths` other paths (1,024 by default) as subcolumns, and the rest in shared data ([JSON type](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/data-types/newjson)). The entry declares five typed paths and sets `max_dynamic_paths = 0`, so every other field, the post text included, goes to shared data, written as `map_with_buckets` in the parts that inserts create and as `advanced` in merged ones. Since 25.8 the advanced format also stores a copy of the data in the original format, which, in the words of ClickHouse's blog, "effectively doubles the storage requirement" ([JSON data type gets even better](https://clickhouse.com/blog/json-data-type-gets-even-better)). The previous post's sample of the 26.11 table found 94 to 102 bytes a row in fresh parts and 191 to 199 in merged ones; LynxDB's store takes about 92. ClickHouse also stores JSON paths flattened but forms nested objects again on output, where LynxDB returns the dotted paths as they are.

## The hash path, before and after 8655937b

Without a sort key, Q2, Q3 and Q5 group rows in hash tables ([exec/agg_partition.go](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/pkg/colstore/exec/agg_partition.go)). Each scan goroutine fills a table of its own, up to 65,536 groups, and then hands groups on. Where they go changed on 24 November.

Before, a goroutine appended each handed-on group, as its hash, key and state, to a private log split into 256 hash partitions, and logged each (value hash, group) pair of a distinct count the same way. The 32 logs lived until the scan ended, when the partitions were merged one at a time. A log grows with every row whose group did not fit the table, so memory grew with the rows scanned, however few the groups.

Since commit 8655937b the logs are staging buffers under one budget, 1 GiB for all goroutines together and as much again for distinct values. A goroutine that has spent its share merges what it holds into hash partitions that every goroutine shares: eight per goroutine, between 256 and 4,096, so 256 on 32 vCPUs, each a table behind a mutex. Distinct values go into per-partition sets of 128-bit MurmurHash3 hashes. A table slot holds a 16-bit fingerprint and the key's place, and keys live in chunks that never move, so a table grows without copying them.

**Before** (main 400bddbb)

**32 scan goroutines**: a table each, up to 65,536 groups

**A private log each**: 256 partitions each, kept until the scan ends

**Merge after the scan**: one partition at a time

*   peak, top accounts **38.71 GiB**

**After** (8655937b)

**32 scan goroutines**: a table each, up to 65,536 groups

staging, 1 GiB for all

**Shared hash partitions**: 256, a table and a mutex each, filled during the scan

*   peak, top accounts **13.48 GiB**

_Where a hash aggregation's groups go once a goroutine's table is full, before and after commit 8655937b, drawn for the 32 scan goroutines of an m6i.8xlarge. The peaks are the server's VmHWM on the cold try of the previous post's top-accounts query (events per `did` , top 10), 1B store without a sort key (24 November 2026)._

The previous post showed the peaks; with the cold times they are:

| Query, no sort key, 1B | Peak before | Peak after | Cold before | Cold after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Top accounts | 38.71&nbsp;GiB | 13.48&nbsp;GiB | 12.16&nbsp;s | 11.95&nbsp;s |
| Q2 | 25.12&nbsp;GiB | 14.50&nbsp;GiB | 14.38&nbsp;s | 13.48&nbsp;s |
| Distinct accounts | 23.23&nbsp;GiB | 12.90&nbsp;GiB | 9.75&nbsp;s | 9.21&nbsp;s |
| Q5 | 19.54&nbsp;GiB | 15.73&nbsp;GiB | not taken | not taken |

The same commit built with a budget too large to reach went back to 37.38, 25.11, 23.23 and 18.82 GiB and ran 8 to 10% faster hot, so the budget is what cuts the memory, at a small cost in time. I expect most of the 13 to 16 GiB that remain to be the groups and distinct values themselves and the blocks being decoded; I have not split it.

ClickHouse aggregates in hash tables too, with more than 40 specializations chosen by the key's types, and can spill a `GROUP BY` to disk past `max_bytes_before_external_group_by`, which is off by default ([GROUP BY](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/select/group-by)). LynxDB has no spill: the budget bounds the staging, and the shared partitions grow with the groups.

## What the design costs

Every block keeps metadata in memory for as long as the server runs: its 52-byte index entry, first key, key runs, filter entries and time records. It grows with the number of blocks whatever the queries are, and on the 1B store it is most of the 151 MiB read at startup. Token filters take 7.88 GB on disk whether anyone searches text or not; ClickHouse writes a skip index only when a table declares one.

With the sort key, text search reads more (a rare word read 1.6 GB with the key and 0.7 GB without), time windows get neither minute records nor block time bounds, and counting from key runs needs one key-ordered stream, which the store has only after its final merge. The previous post measured each of these.

No copy of the original JSON is kept, and events come back flat: `{"a": {"b": 1}}` and `{"a.b": 1}` are the same event to LynxDB, and a field that changes type becomes two columns. The hash path cannot spill to disk and, at 1B without a key, still peaks at 13 to 16 GiB.

ClickHouse has tools that LynxDB lacks: projections and materialized views that do a query's work at write time, skip indexes chosen per column, an inverted text index among them, sort and partition keys that are arbitrary expressions, and a `GROUP BY` that spills to disk. VictoriaLogs' daily partitions and streams make short time windows cheap, which LynxDB's single long partition does not.

I have not measured the footer size of the 1B store beyond the startup read, or Q2 while runs still overlap before the final merge. The code is in [lynxbase/lynxdb](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb), and its [storage](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/docs/site/docs/architecture/storage.md) and [indexing](https://github.com/lynxbase/lynxdb/blob/main/docs/site/docs/architecture/indexing.md) documentation covers the same structures for operators.

[^dict]: An index created with the `part_dictionary` setting, off by default, writes format version 17, which adds per-part string dictionaries before the directories. The benchmark store has none.
